card: Two days earlier, after a first night in a supplementary coach with four passengers, Hegel reached Halle at midday, fetched Hinrichs, ate and slept in the afternoon; at 6 p.m. he left for Nordhausen with one student and slept most of the night. The previous day, from 6 a.m., he travelled with students from Nordhausen to Kassel.
X:
Kassel, August 19

My dear Marie,

I have arrived in Kassel safely. The journey was lively, though not exactly comfortable. After half a day in Halle with Hinrichs and a short sleep, we drove to Nordhausen at night. Yesterday morning at six o'clock the journey began with the students. One talks a lot in the carriage, and the young people are cheerful.

Here in Kassel it is cool in the evening. I have drunk a small cup of wine and am now tired. The landscape along the way was beautiful, but the most important thing is that I am safe.

Greetings to Karl and Immanuel. Kiss the children from me.

Your G. W. F. Hegel
Y: The journey itself so far has certainly not been without discomfort; the first night was the worst, it was far too cramped in the cabriolet, — I moved into the side-chaise, where, however, we were four, and at every station we got a different and always a worse one. From Wittenberg it went better. — At noon we arrived in Halle, the company had diminished; I fetched Hinrichs, ate lunch, slept very well in the afternoon, — at 6 we departed for Nordhausen, only one student with me — an excellent express coach — each person took a side, the bench was like a sofa, I settled myself on it and, as you know, I am accustomed to sleeping on the sofa, slept almost the whole night. — Yesterday and the day before yesterday the most beautiful weather, — but in the first night it rained very heavily from midnight on; — always in the company of students we made the journey from Nordhausen to here yesterday from 6 in the morning.

card: Hegel visited Schönbrunn again in the afternoon, including the menagerie grounds, where he saw only the elephant and the ostrich because the others had already retired for the night. It was too dark to see the plants. In the evening, with no Fodor, Dardanelli or Lablache performing, he saw part of a Leopoldstadt theatre piece and brought away the playbill.
X:
Dear Marie,

This afternoon I was in the Schönbrunn Garden. The air was pleasant, but the plants were barely visible in the dark. In the menagerie I saw only the elephant and the ostrich; the others had already withdrawn to their night quarters. It was a quiet hour, far from the hustle and bustle of the city.

In the evening I looked for music, but Fodor, Dardanelli, and Lablache were absent. So I went to the Leopoldstadt Theatre, where I saw part of a comedy. It was not the high opera we are accustomed to, but the audience was in good spirits. I have brought the program with me so that you can see it.

The journey is tiring, but the variety does good. I think of you and the boys at home.

Your G. W. F. Hegel
Y: All the rooms in Berlin, Potsdam, and Sanssouci, where I wanted to see something, cost one ducat — or should cost! I will advise my acquaintances who might like to see works of art to take the ducats and thalers that are required for everything and anything — even the grave not only of Frederick the Great but also of his dogs in Sanssouci — and use them to cover the travel expenses to Vienna, and then see here the most magnificent treasures, more in reality than they can currently see in Berlin. — Read some of this to my so dear and worthy friend, Privy Councillor Schulze, — precisely so that he may rightly perceive my gratitude from it for all the love and goodness that has come to me through his benevolent, heartfelt interest, and assure him that, despite all the above, I have given the professors here the opportunity to see that we have no one to envy — on the contrary! — But in order to forcibly return to my report, I briefly report that this afternoon I visited the beautiful Schönbrunn with its views once more, also the menagerie, though only the layout and of the beast population only the royal ones, the elephant and the ostrich, — the rest of the rabble had already gone to sleep. Likewise the plants, and since the flowers do not show themselves with a lantern, I have also spared this for another time — finally — today no Fodor, no Dardanelli, no Lablache, no etc.! The end is bad — everything is bad, namely still a piece of a Leopoldstheater piece, of which I bring the slip. — Tomorrow at the crack of dawn onto the galloping carriage — God guide the driver! This is all that the wishes of my breast are limited to for the time being

card: Hegel arrived in Luxembourg by diligence; Herr von Hanfstengel took him on a walk through the town and part of the fortifications. He booked the diligence to Metz for the next morning. A fellow passenger from Löwen, returning from a Rhine tour after losing a son of 21 and a daughter of 17, invited Hegel to visit him there.
X: I have been here for an hour; I drove here in good company. I am here beyond the German border, but not yet within the French one; nor is even that exact, for this part of the Netherlands still belongs to the German Confederation. — I am returning tired from a walk that Mr. von Hanfstengel led me on, through the town and a part of the fortifications. The latter are admirable, so that I can see it too; — I have registered for the diligence to Metz and will depart there tomorrow morning, and from there it goes on to the real goal of the journey, to which the previous part was the preludes. You see that I am not exaggerating. The physical fatigues are not significant, the mental ones consist in the lack of business and the lack of conversation with you, in contrast to a conversation with insignificant company; yet this also goes quite well overall; a good Brabantine from Louvain, who had made a tour to the Rhine to distract himself from the recently suffered loss of a son of 21 years and a daughter of 17 years, was today with us in our diligence, a composed, restrained man, who invited me to visit him in Louvain.
Y:
My dear Marie,

I arrived in Luxembourg today and walked through the city and over part of the fortifications with Mr. von Hanfstengel. It was a pleasant walk.

A fellow traveler from Liège, who is returning from a trip along the Rhine, told me of his great sorrow: He lost a son of 21 and a daughter of 17. He invited me to visit him there.

I have booked the diligence to Metz for tomorrow morning. The heat is subsiding, and I look forward to continuing the journey.

Yours
Hegel

card: The previous morning Hegel and his companion had crossed the Scheldt into Antwerp, a city of 60,000 to 70,000 inhabitants, as is Ghent. He visited the cathedral, whose nave has 3 rows of columns on each side and no pews or benches; each visitor takes one of a stack of 100 chairs and carries it from altar to altar.
X: Yesterday morning we crossed the beautiful, broad, stately Scheldt into the great Antwerp, again with 60–70,000 inhabitants; Ghent has just as many. In these cities one must see the churches! In Antwerp the world-famous Cathedral—in the nave of it, as in the unfinished cathedral in Cologne, 3 rows of columns on each side; how spacious and free one wanders about in it!—The spaces are not blocked up with church pews and benches, there is no bench in it, everything free, but there stands a pile of 100 chairs stacked up, of which each person who comes has one given to them, carries it from one altar to another;—here a small group, there a crowd, always changing, coming and going. The Hague, 9th Oct. Evening.
Y:
My dear Marie,

I am now sitting in The Hague and writing to you briefly about how today was in Antwerp. We crossed the Scheldt and arrived in the city, which, like Ghent, has a population of sixty to seventy thousand souls.

I found the cathedral particularly strange. The nave has three rows of columns on each side, but there are neither benches nor pews. Instead, there are stacks of a hundred chairs there. Every visitor must now take a chair for himself and carry it from altar to altar. One can imagine the crowd dragging things back and forth to follow the service. It is a sight one does not forget so quickly, and it makes the spaciousness of the church lively in a very peculiar, almost restless way.

The evenings are cool here, but the company is friendly. I hope Karl and Immanuel are keeping up their end.

Your faithful
Georg Wilhelm

card: Hegel walked in the park along the Ilm. At 2 p.m. he dined at Goethe's, seated beside him, with Fräulein von Pogwisch, Hofrat Vogel, Dr. Emmerich (Goethe's secretary), the two grandsons, Goethe's son and Zelter; Frau von Goethe, expecting her confinement, was absent. Hegel told Goethe about politics and literature in France. That evening he went to the theatre.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am now sitting in the inn in Weimar and writing to you briefly from the park by the Ilm, which was lovely today. At around two o'clock I was at Goethe's table, seated right next to him. Mrs. Goethe was absent, as she is due to give birth soon, but the company was numerous: Miss von Pogwisch, Court Councillor Vogel, Dr. Emmerich, the two grandchildren, his son, and Zelter.

We spoke a great deal about politics and literature in France; Goethe listens attentively and asks about the latest trends there. It was a pleasant, quiet gathering.

In the evening I was at the theater. The evening is now quiet. Think of me.

Yours
Hegel
Y: I had to take possession of the [illegible/abbreviated term], in order to encounter it. — Then a walk along the old, familiar paths of the beautiful park, trodden 25 years ago, greeting the banks of the little Ilm and its quieter waves, which have heard many an immortal song. At 2 o’clock to lunch at Goethe’s, which was excellent and honored by the best appetite; — Mrs. von Goethe!) is, expecting her delivery every hour, invisible, — so she was not at the table, — the sister, Miss von Pogwisch), quite lively, Court Councillor Vogel the doctor, a Mr. Emmerich), Goethe’s secretary, the two grandchildren, the son, Zelter and I — I sat next to Goethe, on my right the aforementioned Miss; the Weimar guests quieter, but we cheerful, conversational, eating and drinking bravely, — I had to tell Goethe a great deal about the political and literary views and interests in France, he was very interested in everything; he is quite strong, healthy, generally the old, i.e. always young — somewhat quieter — such a venerable, good, faithful head, that one forgets the great man of genius and inexhaustible energy of talent; we are as old, faithful friends anyway not on the footing of observation, — how he appears or what he has spoken, but cordially together, and not for the sake of boasting and honor, that of having seen and heard him, etc. — The son told me very explicitly after the meal how Goethe had rejoiced in the hope that I would call on him on my return journey from Paris; he spoke to me in general in detail about his relationship and feelings towards his father in every respect, and one must praise Goethe in his age and way of life as happy, knowing him in such love and care, and respect and love the son for it. This evening I was then also at the theater, — and now I am writing this to you, — and what I have principally to add is about our plans or rather decisions, finally to go home. Goethe would therefore have Zelter and me with him at least tomorrow; so we travel the day after tomorrow; Zelter just as satisfied that I am with him, as I am that he makes the further journey with me. But since we are both old gentlemen by now and convenience is agreeable and useful to us, we are not inclined to the bravery of the express post,... but we will depart on Friday with the hired coach, which we have already hired, and, if God wills, arrive at your place on Sunday, where your Odysseus, after the multicolored voyages, will return to the monochromaticity of domestic life (returning!) to embrace you.

card: Hegel obtained his ticket for the express coach. The day before, he had been told that all seats for Tuesday and Friday were taken, though passengers could still apply for extra coaches. When he enquired that day, three people from Prague applied at the same time, but for Wednesday rather than Tuesday, so he took a seat for Wednesday.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am sitting in Vienna and writing to you briefly, for time is precious. I have finally received my ticket for the express coach. As late as yesterday, it was said that the seats for Tuesday and Friday were fully booked, but that one could apply for additional coaches. So I inquired today. As chance would have it, three gentlemen from Prague applied at the same time, but they wished for Wednesday, not Tuesday. Since I was free on Wednesday, I immediately took the seat for myself.

So I am leaving on Wednesday. The matter was a little confusing, but now it is settled. I am enjoying the evening here and hope that Karl and Immanuel are well. Kiss Ludwig.

Yours
Hegel
Y: Now all uncertainty has finally been put to an end, and I have the express coach ticket in my pocket. — Yesterday I received the answer that all seats for Tuesday and Friday were taken, but that persons might perhaps still be found for separate coaches. — Upon today’s inquiry, three Prague residents presented themselves along with me, but instead for Tuesday — for Wednesday; so I had to, against my will — but to be certain of the matter — concede one day. In 36 hours I shall then be in Prague and half the distance closer to you, — if only this second half could be covered just as quickly, to be soon with you, my dear, and among you, — there first to rest with you — to tell you — though little will remain that I have not already told in writing — to let you tell me all the more — and also to work.

card: Hegel left Prague after 11 o'clock and travelled in sunshine through the Bohemian countryside and its villages. By evening there was a full moon. He expected to reach Töplitz at noon the next day and Dresden the following evening, or perhaps only on Sunday.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am now traveling through Bohemia. The sun shone all day over the villages and fields, a wonderful sight that somewhat alleviated the fatigue of the journey. I left Prague after eleven o'clock and am enjoying the quiet of the landscape.

A full moon will rise, which will brightly illuminate the night, perhaps making the ride to Töplitz more pleasant. I hope to arrive there at noon. From there, I will continue on to Dresden. Whether I arrive there in the evening or not until Sunday depends on the post stations.

I am cheerful and in good health. Think of me when you read the news in Berlin.

Your faithful G. W. F. Hegel
Y: From Prague I traveled through Bohemia, which is so beautiful in its views—though the Bohemian villages are wretched and no longer seem Bohemian to me now—in the most beautiful, loveliest sunshine, which beautifies everything, just as the full moonlight and a few thin candles now gild my memory of you. Tomorrow at noon I will arrive in Töplitz, and tomorrow evening, perhaps not until Sunday, in Dresden.

card: The previous day Hegel visited Versailles and the Grand and Petit Trianon. The Trianons are furnished; the palace is not. The garden has 130 marble statues, and the oldest tree in the orangery was planted in 1420. The Trianon grounds are in the English style, with artificial rocks and Swiss cottages. He did not see the fountains play.
X:
My dear Marie,

I hope this finds you well, along with the boys. We are in Paris at last. The air is cooler than I expected, though the heat still lingers in the evenings. I have had my usual glass of wine and am writing by candlelight.

Yesterday I went to Versailles. It is a vast place, but strangely empty; the palace itself is unfurnished, just bare halls and echoes. However, the Trianon is quite different. It is fully furnished, and the grounds are laid out in the English style, with those artificial rocks and little Swiss cottages that the French seem to love. I counted the statues in the garden—there are one hundred and thirty of them, all marble. In the orangery, I saw the oldest tree, planted in 1420. It is hard to imagine it standing there for four hundred years, but it is still green and strong. I did not catch the fountains playing, as they were not running when I was there.

I am tired from the walk. I shall rest now.

Your affectionate
Georg Wilhelm
Y: Yesterday I was in Versailles and saw the splendors there, including the Grand and Petit Trianon. The latter two are furnished, but the Palace of Versailles is not, so one sees only the splendor of its doors, walls, ceilings, and wall paintings. The latter are mostly entirely new and mediocre. The gardens are too old-fashioned French: wide squares with clipped hedges, groves, separate side plantings of trees, fountains, statues, colonnades, and so on. The number of marble statues in the garden is 130. The orangery is admirable, and the oldest tree was planted in the year 1420. In contrast, the Trianons have English, charming layouts, though also with whimsical artificial rocks and Swiss-style cottages. The greatest fuss is made about the jumping of the water, which we did not see, only the multitude of Neptunes, Tritons, frogs, and so on.

card: Hegel and Mr. van Ghert walked the Waterloo battlefield for 3–4 hours on Friday and on Saturday saw the Brussels gallery, St. Gudula church and Laeken palace. On Sunday afternoon they went to Ghent, attended the university's rectorate handover there on Monday until 1 o'clock, then left by cabriolet at 2:30, reaching the Scheldt bank opposite Antwerp after 10 pm.
X:
Antwerp, 8 October 1822

My dearest Marie,

The journey has been wearying, but the mind has found its rest. We walked the field of Waterloo for four hours, the ground itself a witness to the turning of ages. It is a place where the spirit of the world felt its weight. In Brussels, the gallery and the church at Laeken offered a different kind of stillness, though the rectorate handover in Ghent was a necessary formality.

We left Ghent late, and the cabriolet carried us through the night. It is now past ten, and we are on the bank of the Scheldt, opposite the city. The air is cool, and the river dark. I am tired, but the road has been clear. I hope the boys are well and that your health is steady. I shall write again once we have settled.

Your devoted,
G. W. F. Hegel
Y: It has been a few days since I have had the first quiet hour in which I am alone and can continue the account of my journey to you, my dear. On Friday we visited the battlefield of Waterloo in a carriage, and I saw here these eternally memorable fields, hills, and points—especially the high, wooded hill stood out to me, from which one can see many miles in every direction, where Napoleon, the prince of battles, had set up his throne, which he lost here! In the stifling midday heat we walked for three to four hours on the paths, where under every clod of earth brave men lie buried. On Saturday we saw the picture gallery, strolled in the park, visited St. Gudula’s Church, and examined its beautiful windows—the most beautiful I have ever seen—its paintings, marble statues, and so on. Then in the evening we went to Laeken Palace—a pleasant walk and a nice spot. On Sunday morning was spent with going out, visiting churches, shopping for you, my dear, and packing, and at half past two o’clock we drove together—Mr. van Ghert had the kindness, and coincidentally also, as a convalescent from an illness, the leisure to accompany me—to Ghent. Here we saw the beautiful cathedral, some other churches, and then attended the act of the handover of the rectorship of the university, which lasted until one o’clock, then quickly ate lunch, and at half past three o’clock drove here in a carriage, where we arrived yesterday after ten o’clock, just opposite from here, on the other bank of the Scheldt.

card: Hegel reached Vienna after 6 the previous evening, travelling 42 miles from Prague in 36 hours by express coach with a couple returning from Karlsbad and Archduke Charles's physician. He took a room at the Erzherzog Karl, went to the Italian opera, a Mercadante piece with Rubini, Donzelli, Lablache and Eckerlin, and then found Lilli and Klein at the inn.
X:
Vienna, September 21

My dear Marie,

I have arrived here safely. The journey from Prague was a hurried affair; in thirty-six hours we covered forty miles. Sharing the coach with us was a couple returning from Carlsbad, and the personal physician of Archduke Charles.

The household of Archduke Charles is hosting me. Today I was at the Italian opera house. They performed an opera by Mercadante, and the voices were remarkable: Rubini, Donzelli, Lablache, and Eckerlin. The evening was short, but the music was good.

On my return, I found Lilli and Klein already at the inn. We sat together and chatted. It was a quiet end to the day. I am well and think of you.

Your
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: Good morning, my dear! — in Vienna — yes, Vienna; — but unfortunately you are not in Vienna.... So, to get to Vienna, I stayed until Saturday afternoon — up to that point, the report of my last [journey] is in Prague. — Everything in order, we drove out of the gate at 6 in the morning (the express coach tripled). The main coach, mine, is divided into two rooms, which are connected by a kind of window, with 4 persons in each. My 3 companions were a gentleman and his wife, returning from Carlsbad, the third being the personal physician to Archduke Charles for 24 years, who had now retired into an independent position, — so that we were very satisfied with one another on all sides and covered this road of 42 miles in 36 hours, up hill, down dale — day and night on, back and forth. Bohemia — monotonous, fertile farmland, — then through a piece of Moravia, Collin, Czaslau, Iglau, Znaim, — then into proper Austria, — here wine country, fields, hills, forests, one place after another, wide views into these rich regions, a splendid land — at the penultimate station we came near the Danube, — without yet seeing it, — onto a low plain, so for half a day on, — monotonous, one has no view of Vienna here, — after 6 o'clock in Vienna itself, then toll, post, — cab, to look for an inn, received a room in the Erzherzog Karl facing the courtyard, one flight up, — those facing the front are not for us; when I asked about Mr. D. Parthey, it turned out that the young married couple Klein!) were lodging here, but had just gone out; — I then accepted a porter and in travel grime (the trunk is still at the toll house, at 7 o'clock I had arrived at the inn), at ¼8 — to the Italian Opera, for Mde Milder, whom I must mention again later, had so commanded?). — A piece by Mercadante, Mde Fodor does not appear in it — but what male voices! Two tenors, Rubini and Donzelli, what throats, what manner, sweetness, volubility, strength, tone, one must hear it! — a duet of theirs of the highest force. The bassist Lablachen) had no leading role, but even here, how I had to admire his beautiful, powerful, as well as sweet bass voice. Yes, these male voices one must hear, that is tone, purity, strength, complete freedom, etc., etc. They also have a German singer, she is called Eckerlin, who has beautiful, full, strong middle tones, which reminded me of Milder, yet only Mde Milder could match those three male voices and keep them in check. Mde Fodor will play in Othello today. — As long as the money lasts to pay for the Italian Opera and the return journey, — I will stay in Vienna! After the opera and a pas de deux by 2 Parisians — all as good as the Berliners, — if the Berlin women would only stretch out a right angle, up to the obtuse — home, where, to our mutual heartfelt pleasure, I found Lilli and Klein (Parthey's young wife was unwell in her room); that is now very pleasant to me, they are staying here this week and we have already engaged to go around together; they were surprised that I come from the Italian Opera, they have been at the Casperl and German theater every evening for three days and have not yet seen the Italian Opera!! and not yet heard it!! This morning it goes to Belvedere (imperial picture gallery), to the post — to collect letters from you, to the toll house, — to settle passport matters.

card: On Sunday Hegel drank at the Töplitz spring, walked in the Clary park, bathed and went up the Schlackenberg again, then left by carriage at 11. He crossed a range of hills in about 1½ hours, with a view to Lowositz, then crossed the Eger twice, the second time by moonlight, towards Meldros. On Monday he reached Prague at 11.
X:
My dear Marie,

I will arrive in Prague today at eleven o'clock in the morning. The journey went smoothly; we crossed the Eger twice, the second time in the moonlight, on the way to Meldros. Yesterday in Töplitz I drank from the spring, bathed, and strolled in the Clary Park. The ascent to the Schlackenberg was laborious, but the view of Lowositz from the carriage, while we drove through the chain of hills in an hour and a half, compensated for the exertion.

The city here is lively. I spent the day with a quiet meal and a glass of wine. The heat abated as the sun set. I think of you and the boys in Berlin. The roads were long, but the spirit is fresher from the movement.

Greetings to Karl and Immanuel.

Your
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: On Sunday I still drank from the fountain, then went to the beautiful Clary Park, then took a bath, then went once more to the slag heap to finally take in the charming view, — then got into the carriage at 11 o'clock, — first over the second of the mountain ranges mentioned above, — everything fertile, rich, varied, — hills full of fields, meadow valleys, villages, fruit trees; after the mountain had been crossed in about 1 ½ hours, it goes from now on downhill or level (except for some small elevations) to Prague, — from the height of the mountain, into this other plane, an unbounded view to Lowositz, just as varied and rich, — from here flat country, boring fruit fields, — twice over the Eger — the second time with the most beautiful reflections of the moonlight towards Meldros. — Today through equally boring country, until the point where I suddenly looked down into the Moldau valley and onto Prague, — indeed a pleasant view shrouded in fragrance — and arrived there at 11 o'clock. — So I am writing this in Prague, and here there are immediately two interesting points: the one is Uncle, the other a letter from you, which needs to be seen and asked about

card: Hegel and his companion had spent a night at Flamandsch Hooft (Point of Flanders). Their road was paved like the Königsstraße in Berlin, tree-lined, and ran between fields, gardens and meadows; unlike around Aachen and Liège they met no beggars, village children wore shoes, many of them wooden, and stockings, and they passed through a village of 15,000 inhabitants.
X:
My dear Marie,

We spent the night in Flamen Hoofd. The road here is paved like the Kings Road in Berlin, shaded by trees, and winds through fields, gardens, and meadows. It is a different world than around Aachen or Liège. We did not see a single beggar.

The children in the village all wore shoes, many of them made of wood, and stockings. We passed a village with fifteen thousand inhabitants. Everything appears orderly and possessing. I looked at the people's clothing; it is clean and smart. Nothing is lacking. The air is fresh, and I slept well, which was very beneficial to me after this long journey.

I will continue my journey tomorrow. Just let me know how the boys are doing.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel
Y: Michelangelo made it, to see — by Michelangelo! Where else in Germany can one see a work by this master? — But to continue the report, we stayed overnight in Flamandsch Hooft (Tip of Flanders). — It is, as said, a pleasure to travel in this country; all the country roads are paved like the Königsstraße in Berlin, alongside the road are all fruit fields, gardens or meadows, and the highway is planted with trees. — From Aachen to Liège it swarms with beggars, up to here we have not met a single one; one sees adults and children in the villages only well-dressed and playing happily, no child in rags, none without shoes (many wooden shoes) and stockings, — we passed through a village of 15,000 inhabitants. —

card: Hegel travelled from Amsterdam via Utrecht and Deventer, then by post wagon with a gentleman from Hildesheim, Mr. Cludius, reaching Osnabrück at 5 am on Wednesday; there he visited Prof. Abeken and saw the hall of the Peace of Westphalia. He reached Bremen Thursday at nightfall and Hamburg by express post on 18 October, seeing fireworks there that evening.
X:
My dear Marie,

I arrived in Osnabrück this morning at five o'clock by post coach with a gentleman from Hildesheim, Mr. Cludius. There I visited Professor Abeken and saw the hall in which the Peace of Westphalia was concluded. It is a historically significant place, but the journey to Bremen was tiring; I did not arrive until the evening.

Now I am in Hamburg. The evening was pleasant, and I saw fireworks in the sky. That was a nice conclusion to the long journey. I hope the children are well and that you are feeling well in Berlin. I will write to you again soon.

Your
Georg
Y: ...badly balanced), my journey up to now had gone quite happily, though it was marred by the lack of news from you; but now, after I received news of you in Amsterdam, the trouble has struck the journey. So instead of taking the direct route here, the waiters—everything went too fast for me to be able to inquire more precisely—put me on the diligence to Utrecht, where I spent the night. From here it went at half past nine in the morning to Deventer. From Utrecht, which is likewise a beautiful city with a university and charming surroundings—farewell beautiful Holland and Brabant—from here it is all heath, though still covered with shrubbery. In Deventer I spent the night again and got on a genuine German post coach.... It was dear to me not to have been sitting on this coach from the point of its departure, otherwise I would not have been able to spend the previous night in a bed either. — So it went day and night—through desolate heaths, though interrupted by some oases—Bentheim lies on a rocky hill, charming with a magnificent unbounded view over the fertile little country—on; we drank good coffee in Dutch kitchens—if I were to have a house built, I would have such a kitchen installed too—but there was no time for a proper lunch;—it crept slowly along in the sand, or on the better paved road it was even worse. — In this torture chamber we stayed until Wednesday morning at 5 o'clock, when we arrived in Osnabrück?). I gratefully remember my traveling companion, a gentleman from Hildesheim—Mr. Cludius, if I am right—with whom I was quite calm and trusting, in contrast to the previous silent Dutch model chart-makers, who could not speak with me and were equally unwilling to make much conversation among themselves. In Osnabrück I slept a few hours very soundly and then sought out a former Jena auditor, Prof. Abeken), a brother of the Berlin one whom you often met at Partheys', whom I was truly glad to see again, and who accompanied me in the most friendly manner. The surroundings of Osnabrück are quite charming; I also saw the hall where the Peace of Westphalia was concluded;—at about 3 o'clock I got on the diligence going to Bremen, and in Diepholz I parted from my good Hildesheim gentleman, who was going to Hanover. The road was in very beautiful sunshine, which I pitied for having to shine on such steppes—though towards Bremen Dutch green meadows—with the night we arrived there yesterday (Thursday), slept until this morning, from where I transferred myself here by extra post. The heavens rained on the Bremen citizens' October 18th Patriotism this morning; but the evening allowed me to clearly see the Hamburg rockets and other fireworks...

card: The previous day Hegel saw Romeo and Juliet performed by the English company in Paris, with Kemble as Romeo. In this staging Juliet wakes in the last act while Romeo, who has already taken the poison, is still alive. In the first-meeting scene Romeo sits beside Juliet before speaking, and Mercutio jokes with the Nurse when she interrupts them.
X:
My dear Marie,

I was at the theater this evening and saw Romeo and Juliet. The English company performed. Kemble was Romeo. There were two things that struck me as deviating from the play. First: In the first scene, Romeo sat next to Juliet before he spoke. Second: Mercutio joked with the Nurse when she interrupted them. But what surprised me most was the ending. Juliet woke up while Romeo was still alive, after he had taken the poison. He did not die before she opened her eyes, as we know it. It was a strange sight.

The air in Paris is pleasant today, and I felt well. I am writing this to you only because I could not say it immediately in Berlin.

Your G. W. F. Hegel
Y: Yesterday I saw Romeo and Juliet by the English troupe, — Juliet was very good, although not of the first rank, — not as much as Mde. Crelinger 2), — Romeo—Kemble was quite mediocre in the first four acts, without any life, — but in the last one, dreadful, mad, — I have now seen the English fury in its full glory; it is wonderful how they butcher Shakespeare; in the last act Juliet awakens while Romeo is still alive, but has already drunk the poison, — here is a scene in which she becomes completely out of her mind with madness and rages most horribly. — The scene of the first meeting of Romeo and Juliet is butchered in the same way, he already loves her beforehand, sits down next to her on the chair before he speaks to her, and when she is interrupted by the Nurse, Mercutio makes fun of her so that they can stay together and talk longer. —

card: The previous day Hegel and Cousin went from Cologne to Bonn, visiting Windischmann and then, together, Herr von Schlegel. That morning they saw Cologne Cathedral again, the Wallraff collection and the Dying Mary, and ate oysters with Moselle wine. At midday Hegel travelled alone to Elberfeld, crossing the Wupper again, among students smoking pipes.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am now in Elberfeld. Yesterday, my cousin and I traveled from Cologne to Bonn to visit Windischmann and Mr. von Schlegel. In the morning, we looked at the Cathedral in Cologne once more, as well as the Wallraf Gallery and the painting of the dying Mary. We ate oysters with Moselle wine.

This noon, I traveled alone to Elberfeld. I crossed the Wupper again and sat among students who were smoking their pipes. The air is fresh. I have taken a room that I like.

Karl and Immanuel may know that I am safe and well. Until soon.

Your G. W. F. Hegel
Y: Now, however, also about our journey; — I wrote to you from Brussels, — in this letter you will find when we departed, — I believe it was Monday, after we had previously in the evening watched the illumination in the city on the occasion of the Queen’s first appearance — the sister of our King!) — So first via Leuven to Liège — a rich country — the next day to Aachen — saw the Cathedral with lights and [we] sat again on Emperor Charles’s throne, then to Cologne — both short day’s journeys — from Liège to Aachen, especially beautiful and rich countryside, — in Liège as in Leuven and Ghent beautiful university buildings; we looked around at these universities, as a future place of rest, if the priests in Berlin finally drive me out of the Copper Ditch entirely; the Curia in Rome would in any case be a more honorable opponent, than the wretchedness of a wretched priestly rabble in Berlin). So arrived in Cologne on Wednesday afternoon, immediately collected your dear letter, — thereby learned that the express mail only reaches Cassel on Friday, i.e. today, — then still in Cologne, — instead of vegetating in this old, ugly city among curiosities on Thursday, made a detour to Bonn, the dear, old friend Windischmann on my part — and then jointly Mr. v. Schlegel“) — first his house by force — and when he had finally come out of it — visited him with all cordiality and cheerfulness — however, the good or rather most stately — and comfortable arrangement of the house — except for the chicken yard and the peacock perch and their painting and arrangement — I reserve for the oral description; only of a woman, whom one might look for there, there is nothing to mention; yet one does not miss her entirely, for if not female, then something feminine is perhaps already found there. — We could indeed have spent several days pleasantly and seriously (though we are generally not inclined to do so) and interestingly in Bonn. That we spent this morning usefully with another visit to the sublime Cathedral, the Wallraf collection, inspection of the dying Marie etc., eating oysters, drinking Mosel wine etc., — must conclude with the addition, that I then alone arrived here at noon with a second crossing of the Wupper in the company of some student tobacco pipes.

card: Hegel travelled on past towns, many sea-going ships and wide green meadows, in good weather, and arrived in The Hague after 8 in the evening. This was the farthest point of his journey, from which he would turn back, but first he planned to see the North Sea the next day.
X: Things are moving quickly, beautiful roads, beautiful cities, ships on the sea in great abundance — wide green meadows, everything charming, prosperous, — good weather — and it keeps going on — and it keeps going on and wider. But this is the farthest point and now it will have to go back. This evening after 8 o'clock I arrived here, but tomorrow the North Sea must still be seen, one cannot resist this temptation.
Y:
My dear Marie,

I have had a long journey behind me today. The weather was wonderful, and I reached The Hague only after 8 o'clock in the evening. It is the furthest point of my journey, from where I will return tomorrow.

The landscape was very pleasant: many green meadows and numerous ships sailing on the water. It was a peaceful, wide area. I have not yet fully shaken off the fatigue of the trip, but the seclusion does good. Tomorrow morning I will still see the North Sea before I set out on the journey home.

I think of you and of our apartment in Berlin. Please tell Karl and Immanuel that I have arrived safely.

Your faithful
Georg

card: Hegel was in Coblenz, writing at a window overlooking the Rhine, the bridge and Ehrenbreitstein, while eating grapes. He had been to the post office early that morning and found no letter from Marie. It was Immanuel's birthday, and he intended to drink an extra glass to him at midday.
X: Here I sit, my dear, fulfilling my purpose, namely being in Coblenz, sitting by a window that overlooks the Rhine, my darling, the bridge, and Ehrenbreitstein, eating grapes, but what grapes! the sweetest, most delicious—and thinking of you all together and writing to you. I was at the post office this morning, but found no letter from you; in Cologne, however, I hope, if none more from you is addressed here and reaches me, then to find one. — On Immanuel’s birthday I shall drink an extra glass this noon, and as you will also be drinking to my well-being today, — so let it be hereby formally clinked! — But there is no fine weather today for fireworks; you, in any case, are taking proper care of yourself?). — I certainly do not yet know for sure one main thing, yet I can hardly doubt, namely that our dear mother should be among those celebrating and clinking; she will therefore also be included in the image of the table with which I am clinking. — So, general salvo, universal long live!
Y:
My dear Marie,

I am sitting here at the window in Coblenz and looking out at the Rhine, the bridge, and the Ehrenbreitstein. The grapes I am eating are sweet, but I cannot really eat, as the post brought me nothing this morning. I searched in vain for a letter from you.

It was Emmanuel's birthday today. To commemorate him, I drank one glass more at noon than custom allows. The city is peaceful, and the light on the water is beautiful, but the silence makes me thoughtful. The journey is tiring, and I miss our home in Berlin.

I hope you and the boys are well. I will continue my journey as soon as the opportunity arises.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel

card: At 10 o'clock the previous evening, while Hegel was waiting for soup in his room in Kassel, Heinrich Beer and his wife walked in; the meeting was unplanned. Beer was returning directly from Kassel and could tell Marie that he had found Hegel well.
X: Good morning, my dear! I was just thinking last evening, while I was waiting for my bowl of soup, whether I should start writing to you yet — it was 10 o’clock — as whom? — Mr. Heinrich Beer!) — and his wife — entered my room. You can imagine the joy we felt at this so unexpected meeting; since he is going directly back from here, he can tell you that he found me in good health.
Y:
Kassel, August 19

My dear Marie,

I am well, as you will hear. This evening, while I was waiting in my room, Heinrich Beer and his wife came in unexpectedly. He has just returned from here and assured me that he found me well. It was a short, but pleasant encounter.

In addition, the weather today was pleasant for walking, and I strolled through the city a bit. The air here is fresh, which was very refreshing after the heat of the last few days. I also read a little and find the time here quiet.

My sons will surely be glad to hear from me that I am in good health. I often think of you in Berlin and of the work that awaits there. But I am enjoying this short break.

Your
G.W.F. Hegel

card: Hegel passed through Herzberg at midday on Monday, where a country preacher's niece joined him as far as Dresden. On arrival he found Privy Councillor Schulze at his inn and persuaded him to delay his departure by a day. That morning the two visited Böttiger, the picture gallery and Böttiger's lecture, where they went through the antiquities again.
X:
Dresden, September 7

Dear Marie,

I have arrived safely. The way went via Herzberg, where, as chance would have it, the niece of a country parson accompanied us as far as here. A pleasant, harmless little folk, who apparently endure the heat better than we do.

In Dresden I already found Privy Councillor Schulze at the inn. He actually wanted to go on, but I persuaded him to stay another day. We sat with Böttiger this morning and then visited the Picture Gallery. It was a pleasant repetition of the antiquities that we have often viewed, but art loses nothing of its value through repetition.

The evening is quiet. I am writing this only to reassure you.

Your
G. W. F. Hegel
Y: The journey has been ordinary and, despite the change in weather, very bearable; on Sunday the sky was overcast — it rained a few times — until Jüterbog; then on Monday, after midday, I arrived in Herzberg, where I had a country parson invite his niece to keep me company until Dresden; she was not ugly, already well into her years, so insignificant and Saxonly polite that I had little more desire or occasion to speak than if I had been traveling alone; so I think nothing ill of this company; had I, however, become a proper Englishman on my travels, I would not have let myself be talked out of it, but would have kept to myself; but as one is still a bit of a German, I could not refuse, and besides — as we Swabians say — I bought the cat in the sack, and the result was not uneven, but insignificant. — Upon arrival I went straight to the inn, where I heard that Privy Councillor Schulze was lodging (— I naturally took rooms at the Blue Star) — I luckily met him and, after he had already arranged everything for his departure today, persuaded him to stay with me until this evening; we were both greatly pleased to meet.... This morning I went with Schulze first to Böttiger, then to the picture gallery, then to Böttiger’s lecture, where we went through the antiquities again.

card: In Coblenz, Hegel had been shown rooms that were bomb-proof and dry, with the explanations given in local dialect, and had to change into his third shirt of the day. It rained without stopping that afternoon, so he slept. He was going to a meal, meant to visit Government Councillor Lange that evening, and planned Bonn next, then Cologne.
X:
Marie,

The rain here has been unceasing since noon, driving me to sleep rather than walk. It was a heavy afternoon. The landlord showed me rooms that are purported to be bomb-proof and dry, explaining the architecture to me in a dialect I could barely parse. I was forced to change into my third shirt of the day; the damp is relentless.

I have taken the rooms. Tomorrow I intend to visit Government Councillor Lange in the evening, though I am not certain if he will be in. After that, I must proceed to Bonn and then Cologne. The journey is tedious, but the work of the world moves on regardless of the weather. I hope you and the boys are well in Berlin.

Your
Hegel
Y: dialect explained the things; they are very nice rooms, bulletproof and dry. — But I am not dry; I must truly put on the third shirt today; you see that I do not lack in movement, also in marching, and that the hardships keep me in good health. Now it is time for dinner, and although satiated from the delicious grapes, I will still let it taste good to me. Tomorrow I will probably arrive in Bonn; it is raining unceasingly this afternoon, I have therefore overslept; the day after tomorrow to Cölln. Where you should address letters to me, I can hardly tell you anymore; I will not be able to receive an answer to this letter before 12 days, by then I will have long since passed Brussels; to Amsterdam via Emden, later Hamburg.... Greetings especially to Mr. Privy Councillor Schulze; — this evening I intend to visit Mr. Government Councillor Lange.

card: In the morning Hegel visited the picture gallery and the art exhibition and went up onto the Brühl Terrace, where he had also been the day before. He had also spent an hour with Ammon. After finishing his letter he was going back to the gallery and then to Tieck.
X:
My dear Marie,

Dresden is beautiful, but the heat is oppressive. This morning I visited the Picture Gallery and was at the art exhibition. The colors are vivid, yet the mood is melancholy. Afterwards, I went to the Brühl's Terrace. I was there yesterday as well, but today the view of the Elbe was clearer. The wind from the breeze was refreshing.

I sat with Ammon for an hour. We spoke about what is currently being discussed in the city. It is quiet here, but the thoughts are turning. I am not yet tired, but the evening is approaching.

I will now return to the Gallery and then go to Tieck. Please give my regards to Karl and Immanuel. I am thinking of you.

Yours
G. W. F. Hegel
Y: This morning the Gallery and art exhibition; onto the Brühl Terrace, where the view pleased me somewhat better today, yesterday it made little impression on me, — I have had quite enough of Dresden; — not to forget that I spent an hour at Ammon’s, — so today after this letter still to the Gallery and to Tiek. Now I hope in Prague to receive a letter from

card: Hegel spent the whole day on his feet in the Esterhazy gallery and at Schönbrunn, where he ate, and was due at the Italian opera half an hour after writing. The weather had cleared the previous afternoon, and the day was fine and not too hot.
X: I am adding another sheet and scribbling a bit more, although I am dull and tired — from standing and walking all day in the Esterházy Gallery and in Schönbrunn, where I ate; since the Italian opera is about to begin in half an hour, I will not engage in any further reports, only that it cleared up yesterday afternoon, and today the weather is the most beautiful in the world, not too hot and promising consistency. — Flesh and blood have struggled with the will — to hasten to meet you from here on Friday, October 1st; however, you give me permission to stay longer, I have seen and enjoyed everything in the whirlwind; I have been diligent, on my feet all day, and there is still much to see; — in order to preserve the good and create for myself a treasure of memory, I must see it once more, — of course I will not see the Italian opera for a second time; the beautiful, infinitely varied, lovely countryside I have only just experienced today, and savored in what beautiful sunshine.
Y:
Dearest Marie,

It was a magnificent day, at last after yesterday's thunderstorm. The heat was bearable, which one hardly dared to hope for in Vienna. I spent the whole day on my feet, first in the Esterházy Gallery, where the paintings had a particular effect under the clear light, and subsequently in Schönbrunn, where I also had lunch. The grounds are immense, but the walk was good for the legs.

Now I am hurrying to the Italian Opera. I am punctual, as befits a Berliner. Think of me when the curtain falls.

Your G. W. F. Hegel

card: Hegel was lodging in Brussels with Mr. van Ghert, at whose house he had spent the night. On arriving the previous evening he had gone straight to the letter post, but the office was already closed. His only news from Marie so far was the letter he received in Cassel; he would learn within the hour whether more had come.
X:
My dear Marie,

I am in Brussels at the house of Mr. van Ghert, who is taking me in for the night. When I arrived last evening, I hurried straight to the post office, but the counters were already closed. So I had to sleep without any news from home. This morning I learned that since the last dispatch in Cassel, no further letter from you has arrived.

The day here is quiet. The weather is cool, and the city seems somewhat quieter compared to Berlin, although the streets are lively. I have wandered through the lanes for a long time to enjoy the atmosphere. It is a pleasant change after the strain of the journey.

I hope that Karl and Immanuel are well and that school is going well. Please let me know when you read this. I miss you both very much in this faraway city.

Your faithful G. W. F. Hegel
Y: So you see now, my dear, that I am at the end of my journey, that is, approximately at the most distant point of it, — approximately, for there will probably still be a small excursion into the neighborhood, but my main direction will now be home, towards you; but until now I have had no news from you beyond the letter I received in Cassel; last evening I went straight to the post office after my arrival, but the office was already closed; now it will be seen in an hour whether there are letters from you there q.... In the meantime I will only tell you that I am lodged here with Mr. van Ghert, who did nothing else, and spent the night with him and am feeling quite well. — I wrote to you from Cölln. On Sunday morning I had Wallraf’s paintings shown to me now in daylight; among them was the main picture, the Death of Mary, undoubtedly by the same Master Schoreel, from whom the picture of the same subject, which belongs to Boisseree, and which you have also always loved so much, is; — the Wallraf one is smaller, about 2¼ feet high, but wider. The donor on one wing, like the woman on the other, are exactly the same portraits, they were complete old acquaintances to me — the arrangement of the figures in the picture, the position of the bed etc. is different. — After I had attended the service in the cathedral in Cölln and taken my leave of the good people who had received me so friendly, I drove to Aachen in the afternoon, — in good company with an elderly Englishman who had become a German and a lawyer from Cölln, who always carries Goethe’s Faust as his Bible on his person, while at the same time being quite pleased with himself in an unreserved way. We arrived at 10 o’clock at night. In Aachen I saw the cathedral first, sat on Emperor Charles’s chair; there are two marble plates on the sides, also on the backrest, smooth, 1⅛ inch thick;

card: When Hegel got off the express coach in Kassel the previous evening, a young man was already waiting for him on behalf of his father, Conrector Matthias, the father of one of Hegel's students, to invite him to stay at their house. Hegel declined.
X: This is my entire experience since you saw me depart. — Now a request — that you hand one of the copies of my Encyclopedia to Mr. Beer in my name, which I otherwise still reserve the right to inscribe; — I had forgotten to do so before my departure. When I alighted from the express post yesterday evening, a young man was already waiting for me, in the name of his father, the Vice-Principal Matthias, the father of one of my listeners, to invite me to stay with him, which I naturally did not accept. Paper is as far as the matter is exhausted. — In the afternoon or tomorrow morning I will probably set out with a hired carriage. Greet the young ones.
Y:
Marie,

I am writing from Kassel, where I arrived last evening. The heat here is oppressive, though the air is cleaner than in Berlin. I must tell you that I was received with a great deal of courtesy at the inn, but I found it impossible to accept the hospitality of the Conrector Matthias’s house. His son, a young man of some promise, came to me personally with the invitation. I declined politely, but firmly. I am a man of habit, Marie, and I find that I require the solitude of an inn room to settle after the journey. The house was too full of life for my present disposition.

The rest of the day has been spent in quiet reflection. I walked briefly in the park, though the sun was still high. I have taken a little wine and am now resting. I do not intend to remain long; the road calls me forward.

Your loving
G.
